correctness.rationale: After the intervention, the difference from the untreated adult cohort is exactly qA(s) exp[-μ(t-s)]; recruitment is unchanged. Thus the unique optimum is sought by maximizing A(s)H(T-s), with positive q an overall factor, and the derivative has the sign of H(T-s)-D(s), where D=A(s)/(βL_0 exp(-αs)). The explicit D in the result satisfies D'=exp[(α-μ)s][1+(α-μ)a]. In the delayed regime this is positive, including α<μ because a<H(T)<1/μ. The difference starts positive and ends negative, so the unique crossing is the strictly optimal interior time. If a≥H(T) and α≥μ, then D≥a. If α<μ, then D is a convex combination of a and 1/(μ-α)>H(T); in both cases the derivative is negative for s>0, also at threshold equality. At s=T/2 the integral term in D strictly exceeds H(s) for α>0, giving the strict half-horizon bound directly. The sign of the same crossing equation gives the stated strict a, α and T comparisons while interior. At α=0 the equation reduces to exp(2μs)=exp(μT)(1-μa); this is a formal constant-source limit, not the positive-loss cohort theorem. Solving a<H(T) gives all three horizon cases. An independent numerical evaluation of the equal-rate example gave s=0.5624831767 and a benefit ratio of 1.9155763157. value.rationale: The theorem identifies when protecting a recruiting cohort actually changes the timing choice and gives a strict bound and comparative statics across the entire idealized finite-horizon problem.
